front: Opportunity cost per unit, read off a PPC or an output table.
cue: Comparative advantage and moving along a PPC.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>opportunity cost of 1 unit of X</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{opportunity cost of 1 unit of X}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>units of Y given up</mtext><mtext>units of X gained</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{units of Y given up}}{\text{units of X gained}}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn><mtext> tons</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mtext> tractors</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{20 \text{ tons}}{10 \text{ tractors}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> tons per tractor</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2\,\text{ tons per tractor}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Comparative advantage goes to the lower opportunity cost, not the larger output (that is absolute advantage).

cue: Adding up spending on final goods and services.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>GDP</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{GDP}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= C + I + G + (X - M)</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Imports are subtracted; transfers and used goods are left out.

cue: The foreign part of GDP and of aggregate demand.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>net exports</mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{net exports} = X - M</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A negative value (a trade deficit) lowers GDP; it is not a budget deficit.

cue: Comparing living standards across countries or years.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>GDP per capita</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{GDP per capita}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>GDP</mtext><mtext>population</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{GDP}}{\text{population}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: If population grows faster than GDP, GDP per capita falls.

cue: Comparing the cost of the same basket across years.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>CPI</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CPI}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>basket cost now</mtext><mtext>basket cost in the base year</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{basket cost now}}{\text{basket cost in the base year}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The base year is always 100; divide by the base year, not the other way round.

front: The inflation rate: the percent change in a price index.
cue: From two years of CPI or the GDP deflator.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>inflation rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{inflation rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>new index</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>old index</mtext></mrow><mtext>old index</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{new index} - \text{old index}}{\text{old index}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Divide by the old index; a fall in inflation (disinflation) is not deflation.

cue: Turning nominal GDP into real GDP, or the reverse.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>GDP deflator</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{GDP deflator}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>nominal GDP</mtext><mtext>real GDP</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{nominal GDP}}{\text{real GDP}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Real GDP = nominal / deflator x 100: students often multiply instead.

front: A real value (real GDP, a real wage).
cue: Removing the effect of prices.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>real value</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{real value}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>nominal value</mtext><mtext>price index</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{nominal value}}{\text{price index}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use the index of the same year as the nominal value; divide, never multiply.

front: The growth rate of real GDP.
cue: How fast output grows from one year to the next.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>growth rate of real GDP</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{growth rate of real GDP}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>real GDP this year</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>real GDP last year</mtext></mrow><mtext>real GDP last year</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{real GDP this year} - \text{real GDP last year}}{\text{real GDP last year}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use real GDP; growth in nominal GDP mixes output with price changes.

cue: The denominator of the unemployment rate.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>labor force</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{labor force}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>employed</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{employed}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mtext>unemployed</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \text{unemployed}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: People not looking for work (retirees, discouraged workers) are not in it.

cue: From counts of employed and unemployed people.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>unemployment rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{unemployment rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>unemployed</mtext><mtext>labor force</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{unemployed}}{\text{labor force}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The labor force is employed plus unemployed, not the whole adult population.

cue: How much of the adult population works or looks for work.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>participation rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{participation rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>labor force</mtext><mtext>adult population</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{labor force}}{\text{adult population}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Discouraged workers leave the labor force: the unemployment rate falls though no one found a job.

cue: Unemployment at full employment.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>natural rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{natural rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>frictional</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{frictional}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mtext>structural</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \text{structural}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Cyclical unemployment is not in it.

cue: Reading how far the economy is from full employment.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>cyclical rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{cyclical rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>actual rate</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>natural rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{actual rate} - \text{natural rate}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Positive in a recessionary gap, negative in an inflationary gap; at full employment it is 0, not the natural rate.

cue: Every multiplier starts from it.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>MPS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{MPS} = 1 - \text{MPC}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: MPC + MPS = 1, so with MPC 0.8 the MPS is 0.2.

cue: How much real GDP changes per dollar of new spending.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>spending multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{spending multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: With MPC 0.8 the multiplier is 5, not 1.25.

front: The tax multiplier (negative: a tax rise lowers output).
cue: The effect of a change in taxes or transfers.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>tax multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{tax multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{-\text{MPC}}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Its size is always one less than the spending multiplier, and a tax cut raises output.

front: The largest change in real GDP from a change in spending or taxes.
cue: Forward: from a policy or a shock to its effect on output.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mtext>real GDP</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta \text{real GDP}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>change in spending</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{change in spending} \times \text{multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use the tax multiplier for taxes and transfers, the spending multiplier for purchases and investment.

front: The change in spending that closes a gap.
cue: Backward: from a recessionary or inflationary gap to the policy.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>change needed</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{change needed}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>gap</mtext><mtext>multiplier</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{gap}}{\text{multiplier}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Divide, do not multiply; decide the direction first.

cue: How far new excess reserves can expand the money supply.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>money multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{money multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>required reserve ratio</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\text{required reserve ratio}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: A cash deposit does not change the money supply at first.

cue: A bank balance sheet.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>required reserves</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{required reserves}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>deposits</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>required reserve ratio</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{deposits} \times \text{required reserve ratio}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The ratio applies to deposits, not to reserves.

front: Excess reserves: what a bank may lend.
cue: A bank balance sheet.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>excess reserves</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{excess reserves}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>reserves</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>deposits</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>ratio</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{reserves} - \text{deposits} \times \text{ratio}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Required reserves come off first.

front: The most the banking system can add to the money supply.
cue: After a deposit or a bond purchase under limited reserves.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>largest change in the money supply</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{largest change in the money supply}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>excess reserves</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>money multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{excess reserves} \times \text{money multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Multiply excess reserves, not total deposits or total reserves.

front: The real interest rate: the nominal rate minus expected inflation.
cue: Lenders, borrowers and the loanable funds market.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mi>e</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = i - \pi^{e}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Unexpected inflation lowers the real rate a lender earns; i = r + expected inflation.

cue: Money growth and inflation in the long run.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: With V and Y steady, faster money growth shows up as inflation.

front: The government budget balance (negative is a deficit).
cue: Deficits, surpluses and the national debt.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>budget balance</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{budget balance}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>tax revenue</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>government outlays</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{tax revenue} - \text{government outlays}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The debt is the sum of past deficits minus surpluses; a deficit is one year.

front: An exchange rate read the other way round.
cue: Switching between "bels per arl" and "arls per bel".
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>price of B in A</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{price of B in A}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>price of A in B</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\text{price of A in B}}</annotation></semantics></math>
worked: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mtext> bels per arl</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4 \text{ bels per arl}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>0.25</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext> arls per bel</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 0.25\,\text{ arls per bel}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: In the market for a currency, its price is in units of the other currency per unit of it.

front: A foreign price in the home currency.
cue: What an import costs, or what an export earns.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>price in A</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{price in A}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mtext>price in B</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>units of A per unit of B</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \text{price in B} \times \text{units of A per unit of B}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Check the units: bels times arls per bel gives arls.
